discovery.note: The first metal isolated by electrolysis, from molten potash (potassium hydroxide).

nameOrigin: From potash; the symbol K is from Latin kalium (Arabic qali, plant ashes).

radioactive.note: 0.0117% of natural potassium; the largest source of natural radioactivity in your body; used for potassium-argon dating.

elementalForm.description: Each potassium atom gives its lone 4s electron to the shared electron sea. One loosely held electron per atom makes the metal very soft and very reactive.

originNote: Made by oxygen burning in massive stars.
appearance: Soft, silvery metal that tarnishes within seconds in air.
summary: Potassium is a soft alkali metal more reactive than sodium. As the K+ ion it is vital for every living cell, and it is a main nutrient in fertilizers.
uses: Potassium nitrate in gunpowder and food curing
Potassium hydroxide for soft soaps and batteries
facts: Bananas are rich in potassium, so they are very slightly radioactive.
Potassium reacts with water fast enough to ignite the hydrogen with a lilac flame.
biology: Essential: K+ sets the electrical voltage of nerve and muscle cells.
hazards: Reacts violently with water; can form explosive peroxides in storage.

discovery.note: Isolated by electrolysis of lime and mercury oxide; lime itself was used since antiquity.

radioactive.note: 0.187% of natural calcium; decays so slowly it is almost stable.

elementalForm.description: Calcium atoms each contribute two 4s electrons to the shared electron sea around Ca2+ cores.

originNote: Made by oxygen and silicon burning in massive stars and in white-dwarf explosions.
appearance: Silvery, fairly soft metal that turns grey in air.
summary: Calcium is the fifth most abundant element in the crust and the most abundant metal in the human body. Chalk, limestone, marble, bones and shells are all built from calcium compounds.
uses: Calcium carbonate in chalk, antacids and paper
Alloys and getters in vacuum tubes
facts: About 99% of your body's calcium is in your bones and teeth.
The White Cliffs of Dover are chalk made from the calcium carbonate skeletons of tiny algae.
biology: Essential: bones and teeth, muscle contraction, nerve signals and blood clotting.
hazards: Metal reacts with water to release hydrogen; low toxicity.

discovery.note: Found in euxenite and gadolinite; Mendeleev had predicted it as 'eka-boron'.

radioactive.note: Used as a tracer in oil refineries.

elementalForm.description: Scandium atoms pool their three outer electrons (4s2 3d1) in a shared electron sea.

originNote: Made in the final burning stages of massive stars.
appearance: Soft, silvery-white metal with a slight yellow tint in air.
summary: Scandium is a light transition metal, scattered thinly through many minerals. Small additions make aluminium alloys much stronger.
uses: Aluminium-scandium alloys for sports equipment and aircraft
facts: Its existence and properties were predicted by Mendeleev eight years before it was found.

discovery.note: Found in ilmenite sand in Cornwall; named by Martin Klaproth in 1795. Pure metal was first made in 1910.

radioactive.note: Made in supernovae; seen in the Cassiopeia A remnant.

elementalForm.description: Titanium's four outer electrons (4s2 3d2) join a shared electron sea; partly filled d orbitals add strong, slightly directional bonding.

originNote: Made in supernovae of both main kinds.
summary: Titanium is as strong as steel but about 45% lighter, and it resists corrosion. Most of it is used as titanium dioxide, the bright white pigment in paint and sunscreen.
uses: Titanium dioxide white pigment and sunscreen
facts: Bone grows onto titanium implants, a process called osseointegration.
biology: None known; the body tolerates it extremely well.
hazards: Low toxicity; fine powder can burn.

discovery.note: Del Río found it in Mexico but was persuaded it was chromium; Nils Sefström rediscovered it in 1830.

nameOrigin: Vanadís, a Norse goddess of beauty, for its colorful compounds.

elementalForm.description: Vanadium contributes five valence electrons (4s2 3d3) to strong metallic bonding.

originNote: Made mainly in white-dwarf (type Ia) supernovae.
summary: Vanadium is a hard metal mostly added to steel for toughness. Its ions show four different colors in solution, one for each oxidation state.
uses: Vanadium redox-flow batteries for grid storage
Vanadium pentoxide catalyst for sulfuric acid
facts: Some sea squirts concentrate vanadium in their blood cells a million-fold.
biology: Used by some organisms; possibly beneficial in trace amounts for humans.
hazards: Vanadium compounds, especially the pentoxide, are toxic.

discovery.note: Found in the red mineral crocoite (lead chromate).

nameOrigin: Greek chroma, color, for its brightly colored compounds.

radioactive.note: Used to label red blood cells.

elementalForm.description: Chromium has six valence electrons (3d5 4s1, an exception to the usual filling order). Its half-filled d shell gives strong metallic bonding and a high melting point.

summary: Chromium is a hard, shiny metal that resists tarnish. Adding it to iron makes stainless steel, and traces of it make rubies red and emeralds green.
uses: Pigments such as chrome green and chrome yellow
facts: Rubies are red because of a little chromium in aluminium oxide.
biology: Trivalent chromium was long thought essential; this is now doubted.
hazards: Hexavalent chromium compounds are toxic and carcinogenic.

discovery.note: Isolated by reducing manganese dioxide with carbon.

nameOrigin: From magnesia nigra (black magnesia), via Italian manganese.

radioactive.note: Made in supernovae and by cosmic rays.

elementalForm.description: Manganese contributes seven valence electrons, but its half-filled d shell holds them unusually tightly, giving a complex, brittle crystal.

allotropes.name: Alpha manganese
allotropes.note: Complex cubic cell with 58 atoms, stable at room temperature.

bulk.note: The real cell is very complex; the viewer shows a simplified body-centered cubic packing.

originNote: Made mainly in white-dwarf (type Ia) supernovae.
summary: Manganese is essential to steelmaking and to life. Its compounds include the deep purple oxidizer potassium permanganate.
facts: Photosynthesis splits water using a cluster of four manganese atoms.
biology: Essential: needed by many enzymes, including the water-splitting center of photosynthesis.
hazards: Long-term inhalation of manganese dust or fumes damages the nervous system.

discovery.note: Iron from meteorites was used before 3000 BCE; smelting began around 1200 BCE (the Iron Age).

nameOrigin: Anglo-Saxon iren; the symbol Fe is from Latin ferrum.

radioactive.note: Made in supernovae; found in deep-sea crusts.

elementalForm.description: Iron atoms share 4s and some 3d electrons in a metallic sea. Its unpaired d electrons line up in domains, which makes iron ferromagnetic.

originNote: Made as radioactive nickel-56 in supernovae, which decays to iron-56.
appearance: Lustrous grey metal that rusts in moist air.
summary: Iron is the most used metal and, by mass, the most common element on Earth as a whole, since it fills the core. Iron-56 sits near the peak of nuclear stability, so stars cannot gain energy by fusing beyond it.
uses: Steel for buildings, vehicles and tools
facts: The red color of blood and of Mars both come from iron.
When a massive star's core turns to iron, it collapses and explodes as a supernova.
biology: Essential: carries oxygen in hemoglobin and is used by many enzymes.
hazards: Iron overdose is dangerous, especially for children taking iron tablets.

discovery.note: Showed that the blue color in glass came from a new metal, not bismuth.

nameOrigin: German Kobold, a goblin: miners blamed goblins for ores that gave off poisonous arsenic fumes.

radioactive.note: Gamma source for radiotherapy and sterilizing food and equipment.

elementalForm.description: Cobalt atoms share 4s and 3d electrons in a metallic sea; unpaired d electrons make it ferromagnetic.

summary: Cobalt is a hard, magnetic metal used in batteries, superalloys and blue pigments. It sits at the center of vitamin B12.
facts: Cobalt blue glass and ceramics have been made for thousands of years.
biology: Essential as part of vitamin B12.
hazards: Cobalt dust and some compounds are toxic and possibly carcinogenic.

discovery.note: Isolated from a mineral miners called kupfernickel, 'Old Nick's copper'.

nameOrigin: German Nickel, a mischievous sprite, from the ore that looked like copper but gave none.

radioactive.note: Made in supernovae; decays to iron-56.

elementalForm.description: Nickel atoms share electrons in a metallic sea; partly filled 3d orbitals make it ferromagnetic.

summary: Nickel is a tough, corrosion-resistant metal used in stainless steel, coins and batteries. Iron meteorites are mostly iron-nickel alloy.
facts: Earth's core is thought to be about 5% nickel.
biology: Used by some plant and microbial enzymes; not shown essential for humans.
hazards: A common cause of skin allergy; some compounds are carcinogenic.

discovery.note: Used for at least 10,000 years; smelted from ores by about 5000 BCE.

nameOrigin: Latin cyprium, 'metal of Cyprus'; symbol Cu from cuprum.

elementalForm.description: Copper (3d10 4s1, an exception) shares its 4s electron in a free-flowing electron sea, which makes it an excellent conductor of electricity and heat.

originNote: Made by neutron capture in massive stars.
appearance: Reddish-orange, shiny metal that turns green over time.
summary: Copper was one of the first metals people used. It conducts electricity better than any metal except silver, so it wires our world.
facts: The Statue of Liberty is green because its copper skin has formed a patina.
Copper is one of only two metals that are not grey or silvery; gold is the other.
biology: Essential: used by enzymes; octopus and horseshoe-crab blood uses copper instead of iron.
hazards: Excess copper is toxic; copper salts can poison fish.

discovery.note: Marggraf isolated it in Europe; zinc was smelted in India from about the 12th century.

nameOrigin: German Zink, perhaps from Zinke (prong), for its spiky crystals.

elementalForm.description: Zinc shares its two 4s electrons in a metallic sea; its full 3d shell does not take part, so bonding is weaker and zinc melts at only 420 °C.

originNote: Made in massive stars and their supernovae.
summary: Zinc protects steel from rust by galvanizing and is a key part of brass. It is essential for life, used by hundreds of enzymes.
facts: Zinc ions help hold together 'zinc finger' proteins that read DNA.
biology: Essential: in hundreds of enzymes and DNA-binding proteins.
hazards: Breathing zinc oxide fumes causes 'metal fume fever'.

discovery.note: Seen as new violet lines in a zinc ore spectrum; Mendeleev had predicted it as 'eka-aluminium'.

elementalForm.description: Solid gallium is unusual: pairs of atoms share a covalent bond (Ga2 units) inside a metallic framework. This weak packing is why it melts in your hand.

bulk.note: The viewer shows a simplified close-packed lattice.

originNote: Made by neutron capture in massive and aging stars.
appearance: Soft, silvery metal that melts at 29.8 °C.
summary: Gallium melts just above room temperature but boils only above 2,400 °C, giving it one of the longest liquid ranges of any element. Gallium compounds power LEDs and fast electronics.
uses: Gallium nitride blue and white LEDs
Gallium arsenide chips and solar cells
facts: Gallium expands when it freezes, like water.
Mendeleev predicted its density before it was measured, and then corrected its discoverer.
hazards: Low toxicity; it attacks and weakens aluminium.

discovery.note: Found in the mineral argyrodite; Mendeleev had predicted it as 'eka-silicon'.

radioactive.note: 7.75% of natural germanium; decays by rare double beta decay.

elementalForm.description: Each germanium atom shares one electron pair with each of four neighbors, forming a diamond-like covalent network. The bonds are weaker than silicon's, making germanium a semiconductor with a smaller band gap.

originNote: Made by neutron capture in stars.
summary: Germanium is a semiconductor that made the first transistors in 1947. Today it is used in fiber optics, infrared lenses and radiation detectors.
facts: The first transistor (Bell Labs, 1947) was made of germanium.
hazards: Low toxicity; some compounds are harmful.

discovery.note: Arsenic compounds were known in antiquity; Albertus Magnus is credited with isolating the element.

nameOrigin: Greek arsenikon, yellow orpiment (from Persian zarnikh, gold-colored).

elementalForm.description: In grey arsenic each atom shares one pair with each of three neighbors, making puckered layers, and keeps one lone pair. Weak links between layers give it a metallic shine.

allotropes.name: Yellow arsenic
allotropes.note: Made of As4 tetrahedra like white phosphorus; unstable.

bulk.note: Sublimes at 887 K; melts only under pressure (1,090 K at 36 atm). Drawn as a simplified distorted cubic net.

originNote: Made by neutron capture in massive stars.
appearance: Brittle, steel-grey metalloid with a metallic shine.
summary: Arsenic is a metalloid notorious as a poison, yet it is also used in semiconductors and, as arsenic trioxide, to treat a form of leukemia.
uses: Hardening lead in batteries and ammunition
facts: Arsenic sublimes: solid turns straight to vapor at 615 °C.
biology: Toxic to humans; some microbes use arsenic compounds.

discovery.by: Jöns Jacob Berzelius; Johan Gottlieb Gahn
discovery.note: Found in residue from a sulfuric acid plant.

nameOrigin: Greek selene, the Moon (it resembles tellurium, named after Earth).

elementalForm.description: Grey selenium is made of endless spiral chains: each atom shares one pair with each of its two neighbors along the chain and keeps two lone pairs.

allotropes.name: Grey (trigonal) selenium
allotropes.note: Helical chains; the stable form, a photoconductor.

originNote: Made by neutron capture in massive stars.
appearance: Grey metallic crystals, red powder or black glass, depending on form.
summary: Selenium conducts electricity far better in light than in the dark, which made it useful in early photocopiers and light meters. It is essential in tiny amounts but toxic in larger ones.
facts: Brazil nuts are among the richest food sources of selenium.
biology: Essential: part of the amino acid selenocysteine in antioxidant enzymes.
hazards: Toxic in excess; hydrogen selenide gas is very poisonous.

discovery.note: Balard found it in salt-marsh brine; Carl Löwig isolated it independently in 1825.

elementalForm.description: Two bromine atoms share one electron pair, and each keeps three lone pairs. Br2 molecules attract each other strongly enough to make bromine a liquid at room temperature.

originNote: Made by neutron capture in massive stars.
appearance: Dark red-brown liquid giving off orange vapor.
summary: Bromine is one of only two elements that are liquid at room temperature; the other is mercury. It is collected from salty brines and the Dead Sea.
facts: Tyrian purple, the ancient dye of emperors, is a bromine compound made by sea snails.
biology: Possibly needed for collagen in animals; studies are ongoing.
hazards: Toxic, corrosive liquid; its vapor burns eyes and lungs.

discovery.note: Found in the residue left after liquid air boiled away.

radioactive.note: Used to date old groundwater and ice.

elementalForm.description: Krypton has a full octet and normally stays as single atoms. With fluorine, the most electron-hungry element, it forms krypton difluoride, KrF2.

originNote: Made by neutron capture in stars.
appearance: Colorless gas; glows white-violet in a discharge.
summary: Krypton is a rare noble gas. From 1960 to 1983 the meter was defined by the wavelength of light from krypton-86.
uses: High-performance light bulbs and flash lamps
facts: Superman's Kryptonite is fictional; real krypton is a harmless gas.
